metadata.h1: Telecom Site Civil Construction in Papillion, Nebraska
metadata.intro: Papillion is a 24,000-person city carrying hyperscale-class construction demand. Google broke ground on its 275-acre Papillion data center campus in 2019 and has kept investing since — including a $1.2 billion commitment to Papillion and Lincoln announced in 2023 — while Meta's neighboring Sarpy County campus has grown toward nine buildings and roughly four million square feet, and Fidelity's Papillion data center predates them both. All of it runs on OPPD power in the only state that is 100% public power, and all of it sits in Nebraska's fastest-growing county, where a new Springfield Creek interceptor sewer is being built specifically to open the county's southern half — and its next data center ground — to development.

geotech.dominantGeology: Papillion sits on the loess-mantled uplands of the greater Omaha map area: Peoria loess over older Loveland loess and pre-Illinoian glacial till, dissected by the Papillion Creek drainage, with Pennsylvanian limestone and shale and Cretaceous Dakota Sandstone at depth (USGS MF-2391, surficial geologic map of the greater Omaha area; USGS Professional Paper 472).
dominantSoilTypes: Loveland loess / pre-Illinoian till at depth
geotech.expansiveSoilNote: Loess behavior here is a settlement-on-wetting question more than a shrink-swell one; the NRCS shrink-swell grade for Sarpy County was not readable through this environment, so no risk grade is published.

karstRisk.note: No karst hazard mapping for Sarpy County surfaced in the sources reviewed.

geotech.foundationApproachNarrative: Foundation work in Papillion divides by landform. On the loess uplands — where the data center campuses and most new compounds sit — augered piers and spread footings excavate quickly, and the design question is protecting that silt from water: graded drainage, prompt backfill, and covered excavations, because wetted loess gives up bearing strength fast. In the Papillion Creek bottoms the calculus changes to alluvium, shallower groundwater, and flood screening against the NRD's dam-regulated but historically flashy watershed. One local code wrinkle matters to hut and cabinet designers: Papillion's amendments have required frost-protected shallow foundations to be designed and sealed by a Nebraska-licensed structural engineer, which removes the prescriptive FPSF shortcut and pushes small-footprint designs either below frost depth or into engineered territory. Site borings govern; the loess column and the creek alluvium are different worlds a mile apart.

regulatory.permitTimelineNarrative: Jurisdiction is the first question on a Papillion-area site: city, two-mile ETJ, and unincorporated Sarpy County interleave along the NE-370 and Highway 50 corridors, and the answer decides whether plans go to the city's Building Department or Sarpy County Planning & Building on Golden Gate Drive. ROW work inside the city needs the Director of Public Works' written permit with fee, possible bond, and insurance; state-route crossings on NE-370, US-75, or NE-50 add an NDOT District 2 permit. The state stormwater clock — SWPPP, CERT, NOI seven days before grading at one acre — is the same as everywhere in Nebraska, but MS4 oversight through the Papio Partnership adds local erosion-control inspection in this fast-growing watershed.

electricProviders.note: Public power district — a state political subdivision rather than a city department; 'municipal' is the nearest available category. OPPD serves the Sarpy County data center corridor, and its public-power rates are repeatedly cited in operators' siting decisions here.

environmental.listedSpeciesNote: Run the Nebraska Game and Parks CERT and USFWS IPaC per site — the CERT is already a required attachment to the state stormwater NOI, so the screening happens on every disturbing project anyway. environmental.floodplainPrevalenceNote: Papillion is the namesake of the Papillion Creek watershed, where fatal floods in 1964 and 1965 drove the 1968 Flood Control Act's 21-dam authorization; the Papio-Missouri River NRD now operates the resulting dam and detention network plus a 22-gage flood warning system, and a federally approved watershed improvement plan (2024) is adding structures. Mapped floodplain follows the Papio creeks through the heart of the city — creek-adjacent sites get floodplain screening before design starts.

seasonality.narrative: Papillion builds on the same continental calendar as the rest of the Omaha metro — frozen ground roughly December through February, a soft and saturated thaw in March, then a productive April-through-October core interrupted mainly by convective storms. What's locally distinct is the watershed: the Papio creeks are engineered but flashy, so spring erosion-control compliance is policed harder here than in slower watersheds, and creek-adjacent schedules carry March flood-risk contingency. Climate figures should be confirmed against the NCEI normals for the metro stations before publication; hyperscale campus schedules run through winter regardless, with site civil priced accordingly.

costDrivers.rockNote: Thick loess and till overlie bedrock across the uplands; rock tools are rarely mobilized for hut, pad, or duct bank depths in this corridor.
costDrivers.readyMixProximityNote: The Sarpy corridor's sustained data center construction supports metro ready-mix capacity nearby, but hyperscale pour schedules can compete for supply — batch-plant commitments get locked early on campus-adjacent work.
costDrivers.permitFeeNote: Papillion ROW fees follow the Master Fee Schedule, with bonding at the Public Works Director's discretion — small line items, but they belong in the estimate.
costDrivers.prevailingWageExposure: No Nebraska state prevailing wage; Davis-Bacon attaches to federally funded work of $2,000+, including BEAD builds.
costDrivers.seasonalPremiumNote: Winter frost excavation and concrete protection from roughly December through March; March thaw can add undercut and stabilization cost on loess subgrades.
costDrivers.narrative: Cost in Papillion is shaped less by ground and more by the market around the ground. The hyperscale campuses keep local subcontractors, ready-mix, and equipment in demand, so mobilization timing and supplier commitments move numbers in ways a quiet market never sees. The physical drivers are the metro's usual pair — winter protection against frost from December through March, and wet-season loess subgrade risk in the thaw — plus the engineered-FPSF code wrinkle that pushes small foundations either below frost or through a Nebraska-licensed structural engineer's stamp. Creek-adjacent sites add floodplain and MS4 erosion-control cost. Drivers, not prices: every scope prices to its borings, its month, and — in this corridor — its place in the supplier queue.

compliance.stateContractorLicensing: Contractors working in Papillion register with the Nebraska Department of Labor under the state Contractor Registration Act — an annual registration ($40/year effective August 2026) rather than a licensed-GC regime — with out-of-state firms also meeting tax-compliance and surety bond requirements; electrical trades are state-licensed separately.
compliance.insuranceBondingNorms: Papillion's ROW permit requires proof of insurance and, at the Public Works Director's discretion, a bond; railroad right-of-entry adds railroad protective liability coverage.

hazards.designImplications: Sarpy County sits in the heart of the central-plains severe-weather belt: anchorage, hail-rated equipment, and generator fuel containment are designed to convective-season realities, and the Papio Creek floodplain — dam-regulated but historically deadly in 1964–65 — makes creek-adjacent pad elevation a siting decision. Frost governs foundation depth; publish the numeric value only after Papillion's amended code table is read directly.

items.headline: Google commits $1.2B more to Papillion and Lincoln data centers
items.detail: Google announced an additional $1.2 billion investment in Nebraska in August 2023, expanding the Papillion campus and building a new Lincoln facility, on top of the Papillion campus it broke ground on in 2019.

items.headline: Meta grows Sarpy campus toward nine buildings, ~4M sq ft
items.detail: Meta's Sarpy Data Center, first announced in 2017, announced further growth in July 2022 — a ninth building pushing the campus to roughly four million square feet.

items.headline: Sarpy County builds sewer capacity to unlock its southern growth ground
items.detail: The Sarpy County Wastewater Agency secured a $69.8 million Clean Water SRF loan to build the Springfield Creek interceptor and a cooling-water blowdown sewer serving nearby data centers — infrastructure aimed squarely at the county's next development phase south of the ridge line.

items.headline: Nebraska BEAD final proposal approved by NTIA
items.detail: Nebraska's $405.3M BEAD allocation received final-proposal approval in December 2025, with an initial deployment round of about $44.5M federal funding across 29,597 locations statewide.

fiber.narrative: Fiber civil in Papillion is campus-driven: every building Google and Meta add to the Sarpy corridor pulls more metro and long-haul capacity down from Omaha's interconnection core at 1623 Farnam, and those routes cross NE-370, US-75, and NE-50 — all state highways needing NDOT District 2 occupation or crossing permits — plus Union Pacific and BNSF trackage whose crossing approvals run months. Inside the city, ROW work goes through a written permit from the Director of Public Works with insurance on file and bonding at the director's call. The boring itself is friendly — loess uplands with rock tools rarely needed — but the Papio creek crossings put bores under flashy, MS4-policed drainages, so crossing depth and frac-out planning get real attention here.

wireless.narrative: Wireless demand in Papillion tracks rooftops: Sarpy is Nebraska's fastest-growing county, and the subdivisions filling the NE-370 corridor and the ground south toward the new Springfield Creek interceptor all need macro capacity and densification behind them. Papillion's own code stack shapes the civil work — the 2018 I-codes as amended by Ordinance 1934, including the amendment requiring frost-protected shallow foundations to carry a Nebraska-licensed structural engineer's seal, which in practice sends small cabinet and hut foundations below frost depth on most builds. Small cell work in city ROW follows the state Small Wireless Facilities Deployment Act through the city's 2019 telecommunications chapter. Compounds near the Papio creeks get floodplain screening first; the watershed's dam network exists because this drainage used to kill people.

secondaryScopeIds: heavy haul access and crane pads
edge.narrative: This is one of the few Tier 2 cities in our footprint with three named hyperscale-class operators inside or beside its limits: Google's 275-acre Papillion campus (building since 2019, with $1.2 billion more committed to Papillion and Lincoln in 2023), Meta's nine-building, roughly four-million-square-foot Sarpy campus, and Fidelity's earlier Papillion data center. The civil scope that buildout sheds — transformer and switchgear pads, generator yards, campus duct bank, security compounds, heavy-haul access — is exactly what we self-perform. Two local facts govern the next phase: OPPD's public power serves the whole corridor, and the county's $69.8 million Springfield Creek interceptor plus a dedicated cooling-water blowdown sewer are being built to open the ground south of the ridge line, which is where the corridor's next campuses and their edge satellites will need pads.
localSpecificsReferenced: Springfield Creek interceptor / cooling blowdown sewer

operations.mobilizationNote: Papillion rides the same I-80 spine as the rest of our western reach, but with a Sarpy-side finish: crews stay on the interstate to the metro's southwest quadrant and come in through the NE-370 corridor, so equipment and shelter hauls never touch downtown Omaha traffic. In practice that makes Papillion a deploy-and-stay market for the work it actually generates — campus-support scopes and compound builds run as consecutive full days with crews lodged locally, while single-day scopes like a pad pour or vault set are scheduled as early-roll day trips. Shelter and oversize hauls clear NDOT permitting on the state system and finish on the corridor's paved arterials, which carry heavy construction traffic year-round; rural section-road sites are the only thaw-season routing question. Response commitments publish after ops sign-off.

faq.question: Who is the building authority for a telecom site in Papillion?
faq.answer: Inside city limits and the two-mile extraterritorial jurisdiction, the City of Papillion Building Department, enforcing the 2018 I-codes as amended by Ordinance 1934. Outside that, Sarpy County Planning & Building on Golden Gate Drive takes over. Boundaries interleave along the NE-370 and Highway 50 corridors, so we confirm jurisdiction before drawings go anywhere.

faq.question: How deep must a fiber hut or cabinet foundation go in Papillion?
faq.answer: Below the frost line in Papillion's amended code table — a value we publish only after reading the city's amendment text directly, so it stays open here. What is confirmed: Papillion's amendments have required frost-protected shallow foundations to be designed and sealed by a Nebraska-licensed structural engineer, which removes the prescriptive FPSF shortcut and sends most small foundations below full frost depth.

faq.question: Who issues right-of-way permits for utility work in Papillion?
faq.answer: The Director of Public Works. Any building, excavation, or utility installation in or along public ROW needs the director's written permit, with fees per the Master Fee Schedule, proof of insurance, and a bond if the director requires one. Street and curb cuts run through the city's online permitting, and questions go to Public Works at 402-597-2043.

faq.question: What permits do the state highways through Papillion add?
faq.answer: NE-370, US-75, and NE-50 are all state routes, so any utility occupation or crossing on them needs an NDOT permit — Form 19 under the Utility Accommodation Policy — through District 2 in Omaha, which covers all of Sarpy County. A fiber route that runs the growth corridor usually touches at least one of the three, so the district permit is on the critical path more often than not.

faq.question: What data center work is actually happening around Papillion?
faq.answer: Three operators are in the ground: Google's 275-acre Papillion campus, expanding since its 2019 groundbreaking with $1.2 billion more committed to Papillion and Lincoln in 2023; Meta's Sarpy campus, grown toward nine buildings and roughly four million square feet since 2017; and Fidelity's Papillion data center, announced back in 2012. County sewer investment along Springfield Creek is being built to open the next phase south of the ridge line.

faq.question: Is the Papillion Creek floodplain a concern for site selection?
faq.answer: Yes, and it has history: floods in 1964 and 1965 killed residents and drove a 21-dam federal authorization in 1968. The Papio-Missouri River NRD now runs the dam and detention network with a 22-gage flood warning system, but mapped floodplain still follows the creeks through town, and creek-adjacent pads get floodplain screening before any design work starts.

faq.question: Can shelter deliveries reach Papillion year-round?
faq.answer: On the paved corridor, yes — NE-370 and the arterials carry heavy data center construction traffic in every season, and oversize hauls clear NDOT permitting on the state system. The thaw-season caution is rural gravel section roads south and west of the city, where county postings from roughly February into April can force routing changes or a wait for a compound delivery.

faq.question: Who provides electric service for new telecom sites in Papillion?
faq.answer: OPPD — a public power district, since Nebraska is the only state served entirely by public power. New service for huts, compounds, and campus-adjacent edge sites is coordinated through district processes rather than an investor-owned utility's, and OPPD's rates are one of the stated reasons Google, Meta, and Fidelity chose this corridor. Natural gas in Papillion is served by Black Hills Energy under franchise.

faq.question: How much notice does Nebraska811 need before we dig in Sarpy County?
faq.answer: At least two business days, and not more than ten, excluding weekends and holidays — the statewide One-Call Notification System Act standard. Every bore, trench, vault set, and pier hole we schedule in the Papillion area carries that two-day ticket lead, layered ahead of the city ROW permit and any NDOT district permit on the state routes.

decisionGuidance.heading: Building telecom civil scope beside a hyperscale campus in Sarpy County
decisionGuidance.body: The judgment call that distinguishes Papillion work is sequencing around giants. A hut pad or compound that would be a quiet standalone job elsewhere sits here inside a corridor where Google and Meta pour concrete on campus schedules — which means ready-mix capacity, flagging crews, and even NDOT district permit attention are shared resources. Our rules for the corridor: lock batch-plant commitments when the pour date is set, not the week before; file NDOT and railroad crossing applications at award, because a state-route corridor plus two Class I railroads puts multiple month-scale approvals on nearly every fiber route; and confirm jurisdiction — city, ETJ, or county — before producing drawings, since the boundary decides the AHJ and the amendment set. On foundations, assume the engineered-FPSF amendment takes the shallow shortcut off the table and price small foundations at full frost depth unless a structural engineer's sealed design says otherwise. And on any site within sight of a Papio creek, run the floodplain map before the geotech scope — in this watershed, elevation screening is cheaper than redesign, and the NRD's dams exist precisely because the creeks once proved what they could do.
